query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high‐entropy alloy, exposure to high temperatures in oxidizing environments promotes rapid outward diffusion of oxygen and a preferential formation of a continuous, yet brittle, alumina‐rich oxide layer—especially along grain boundaries and minor secondary phases. This scale forms unevenly and generates internal stresses. In reducing environments, the suppressed oxide scale formation shifts degradation to be controlled by the nucleation and growth of internal precipitates at grain boundaries, which embrittle interfaces and induce premature catastrophic failure.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured high‐entropy alloy with a homogeneous fcc matrix and minimal secondary phases in the as-fabricated condition.
generation.intervention: Control of the oxygen partial pressure during elevated temperature exposure, e.g., testing identical samples in environments with high (oxidizing) versus low (reducing) oxygen content.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperatures (e.g., in the range of 700°C–900°C) under either oxidizing or reducing gas environments for prolonged times to capture both surface oxidation kinetics and internal microstructural evolution.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation and distribution of oxide scales along grain boundaries and the emergence of internal precipitates at those boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Under oxidizing conditions, rapid oxygen diffusion causes a preferential formation of a brittle, alumina-rich oxide scale, particularly at grain boundary sites. The resulting internal stresses from the growth and spallation of this scale weaken the alloy’s structural cohesion. Under reducing conditions, limited external oxidation leads to enhanced diffusion of residual reactive species into the interior, promoting the nucleation of grain-boundary precipitates that embrittle the structure, causing catastrophic failure when stressed.
generation.predicted_outcome: In oxidizing gases, samples will develop a continuous but brittle oxide layer (evidenced by increased surface oxide thickness and grain boundary oxidation) which eventually spalls under thermal cycling, whereas in reducing gases, there will be a lower degree of surface oxidation but a higher density of grain-boundary precipitates and microcracking leading to earlier catastrophic failure relative to the untreated (baseline) state.
generation.baseline: The as-fabricated alloy’s microstructure and mechanical properties prior to any high-temperature exposure, which shows uniform fcc matrix characteristics and minimal grain-boundary precipitates or oxide scales.
generation.boundary: This behavior is expected to be relevant under sustained elevated temperatures (approximately 700°C–900°C) with controlled gas atmospheres—specifically, conditions with distinctly high (oxidizing) versus low (reducing) oxygen partial pressures.
generation.uncertainty: The relative contributions of oxide scale-induced spallation versus internal precipitate embrittlement to the overall degradation and catastrophic failure remain uncertain. Additionally, the kinetics of diffusion and the exact threshold oxygen partial pressures that dictate one path over the other may vary.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform a series of high-temperature (700°C–900°C) aging experiments comparing samples exposed to controlled oxidizing atmospheres (with high oxygen partial pressure) with those in reducing atmospheres. Characterize the evolution of surface oxide layers (using SEM/EDS and XRD) and internal precipitate formation (using TEM and atom probe tomography) throughout the exposure period. Concurrently, evaluate mechanical properties and monitor time-to-failure under cyclic thermal or mechanical loading.
measurements: Surface oxide scale thickness and composition
Grain boundary precipitate density and composition
Residual stress measurements in the oxidized layer
Mechanical failure load and time-to-catastrophic failure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the controlled variation in oxygen partial pressure does not result in significant differences in either the oxide layer formation (including its brittleness and spallation) or the development of grain-boundary precipitates (and if these differences do not correlate with differences in mechanical degradation and failure modes), then the proposed mechanistic hypothesis is falsified.
